expected.name: John Hogan
expected.description:
Hogan was one of the Catonsville Nine, a group of Catholic activists whose 1968 draft-records action became a defining moment in Vietnam-era resistance. On May 17, 1968, the group removed 378 files from the draft board office in Catonsville, burned them with homemade napalm in the parking lot, and waited to be arrested.

Tried in federal court that October, Hogan was convicted of destroying government property and interfering with the Selective Service system and was sentenced to two years in prison.

2 years federal prison

expected.name: Daniel Berrigan
expected.description: Daniel Joseph Berrigan, S.J., was a Jesuit priest, poet, and organizer against war and nuclear weapons. A member of the Catonsville Nine, he served 18 months in federal prison after the group burned draft records in 1968. On September 9, 1980, Berrigan joined seven other activists in entering General Electric’s missile plant in King of Prussia, Pennsylvania, where they hammered on nuclear-warhead nose cones and poured blood on documents. The Plowshares Eight action launched the modern Plowshares movement. After a decade of appeals, the defendants were resentenced in April 1990 to time already served.

3-10 years state prison; reduced to time served on appeal April 1990

expected.name: Robert F. Williams
expected.description:
Robert F. Williams was a civil-rights organizer who organized for civil rights in Monroe while insisting that Black communities had a right to armed self-defense against white supremacist violence. As president of the local National Association for the Advancement of Colored People branch, he clashed with more strictly nonviolent strategic approaches and became an emblematic, polarizing figure in debates about whether nonviolence alone could protect people facing terror and impunity.

Williams’ political life was shaped by criminal charges and flight from prosecution. During violence in Monroe in 1961, he became the target of kidnapping accusations tied to a white couple caught up in the unrest, and the FBI sought his arrest—prompting him and his wife to flee, first to Cuba and later to China. In exile he continued activism through political writing and broadcasting, maintaining an international profile while unable to safely return. When he came back to the United States in 1969, the case remained a legal shadow for years; the remaining charges were ultimately dropped in 1976, closing a long chapter in which political activism, exile, and criminal prosecution were tightly intertwined.

John Lewis — Alabama / Georgia

expected.name: Jerry Rubin
expected.description:
Jerry Rubin was a Berkeley anti-Vietnam War organizer and co-founder, with Abbie Hoffman, of the Youth International Party. He helped plan the demonstrations outside the 1968 Democratic National Convention and was prosecuted as one of the Chicago Eight. He later abandoned radical politics and became a Wall Street investor — a transformation that itself became a 1970s cultural touchstone.

The Chicago conspiracy trial (September 24, 1969 – February 20, 1970) prosecuted eight organizers of the demonstrations outside the 1968 Democratic National Convention under the new federal anti-riot provisions of the 1968 Civil Rights Act. The proceedings before Judge Julius Hoffman became one of the most chaotic and politically charged trials in American history. Bobby Seale's case was severed after Hoffman ordered him bound and gagged in court for demanding the right to represent himself; the remaining seven became known as the Chicago Seven. The jury acquitted all seven of conspiracy and acquitted Froines and Weiner on all charges, but convicted Davis, Dellinger, Hayden, Hoffman, and Rubin of crossing state lines with intent to incite a riot.

The defendants were arrested in March 1969, booked, and held in the Cook County Jail before posting bail in the days that followed. During the trial itself Judge Hoffman repeatedly held them in contempt and ordered them taken into custody from the courtroom — Bobby Seale most famously, but the other seven and their attorneys as well, accumulating 159 contempt citations between them. Each convicted defendant was sentenced to five years in prison and a $5,000 fine, with bail pending appeal granted within weeks; the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals reversed all the riot-act convictions in November 1972 and the contempt convictions in May 1972, and the government declined to retry, so the underlying five-year sentences were never served.

expected_cases.charges: Conspiracy and crossing state lines with intent to incite a riot (Anti-Riot Act of 1968); contempt of court (during trial)
expected_cases.sentence: Physical custody from February 15 to February 28, 1970 following contempt commitment, ending with release on bail. Sentenced February 20 to five years and a $5,000 fine on the Anti-Riot Act count; that conviction was later reversed. The appeal period was not continuous imprisonment.

expected.name: Courtney Williams
expected.description: Courtney Williams is a U.S. Army veteran and former Department of the Army employee who supported a special military unit at Fort Bragg and held a Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information clearance. Beginning in 2022, she communicated with journalist Seth Harp, whose reporting and 2025 book “The Fort Bragg Cartel” discussed the unit and described Williams’s allegations of sexual harassment, gender discrimination and retaliation. Federal prosecutors allege that Williams also shared classified information about the unit’s personnel, tactics and procedures. The FBI arrested her on April 7, 2026, and a grand jury indicted her the following day on four counts under the Espionage Act. She remained incarcerated through her April 13 detention hearing, when a judge ordered her released to home detention and location monitoring while the case proceeds. The conditions of release bar her from speaking with the media or using social media.

expected.name: Father Michael Doyle
expected.description: Father Michael Doyle was an Irish-born Catholic priest of the Diocese of Camden, New Jersey, longtime pastor at Sacred Heart Church in South Camden, and one of the Camden 28 defendants. He was one of more than twenty defendants arrested in the early hours of August 22, 1971 during the FBI surveillance and capture of the Camden draft-board raid in progress. He spent brief pretrial detention after the arrest, and the case proceeded to trial in spring 1973 in U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey. On May 20, 1973 a Camden federal jury acquitted all 28 defendants on all counts — the first complete legal victory for the anti-war movement after dozens of Catholic Left draft-board actions. He went on to a 50-year ministry in South Camden focused on housing, food access, and immigrant rights. He died on November 23, 2022, age 88.

Sources: UPI, July 14, 1983; Agnes Bauerlein’s 1987 testimony, reproduced by her son.

Initial AVCO release established

The original Nuclear Resister 19, August 23, 1983, page 1 names Agnes Bauerlein and reports the seven defendants' recognizance release July 22. This dates the initial stay, not the discharge from any later sentence. The earlier group duration estimate is not an individual total. Contemporary report.

Separate December 1983 AVCO detention

The original February 12, 1984 Nuclear Resister, physical page 6 / printed page 5, AVCO Plowshares Guilty, individually names all seven defendants. It reports their December 16, 1983 conviction, sentence, immediate jailing and release later that same day pending appeal. This short post-verdict interval is recorded separately from July 14–22, 1983; the intervening period is not counted as incarceration. Concurrent versus consecutive terms depended on prior records and is not individually assigned without evidence.

The report also distinguishes the December 20 return of John Pendleton and Jean Holladay. That later imprisonment is not assigned to the other five. The contemporaneous report confirms Pendleton's February 6 release but only forecasts Holladay's early-March release, which must not be entered as an exact actual discharge.

expected.name: Karol Schulkin
expected.description: Early Ground Zero member arrested with Shelley Douglass and Mary Grondin walking the warhead rail line into Bangor naval base on Ash Wednesday, Feb 16, 1983. Told the court: "I must stand up and say, no more — no more bombings and burning of people and lands."
expected.body:
1983 arrest, sentence admission and actual release verified

Schulkin was arrested with Shelley Douglass and Mary Grondin at Bangor on Ash Wednesday, February 16, 1983, not February 15. The contemporary March 9 Nuclear Resister reports that the three were initially released with ban-and-bar letters pending arraignment. Arrest is therefore not the start of continuous imprisonment through July. Original arrest and initial release report, printed page 1; Later participant-based account.

The original July 7 issue states that Schulkin was sentenced July 6 to ten days and immediately taken to Pierce County Jail in Tacoma. This establishes both sentencing and actual sentence admission on July 6, replacing the unsupported February admission and generic cite-and-release disposition. Mary Grondin's suspended sentence must not be attributed to Schulkin. Contemporary sentence and jail-admission report, printed page 5.

The August 23 issue reports Schulkin's actual release on July 15 after serving the ten-day sentence. This supersedes the July 17 anticipated release in the earlier roster. Ten days is retained as the source's reported sentence service; July 6 to July 15 is nine elapsed calendar days, and neither counting convention implies uninterrupted custody since February. No independently identified photograph has yet been verified. Actual release report, printed page 6.

Portrait source (October 2026 follow-up): Later-life portrait from People's Self-Help Housing, Karol Schulkin biography; photograph date and photographer are not specified. Identity corroboration: Discover Hollywood's interview identifies Schulkin as an Immaculate Heart Community president and anti-nuclear activist and discusses the community's Housing Works connection. The PSHH biography also identifies her Housing Works board service. This is not presented as a 1983 custody photograph. Source attribution does not imply an open license.

Walter Sprunger was a Mennonite from Adams County, Indiana, who refused military service on religious grounds. (January 1, 1889 - October 15, 1918)

expected.name: Jenny O'Connell-Nowain
expected.description:
Jenny O'Connell-Nowain is a 41-year-old former preschool teacher from Redding, California with no prior criminal history. At a Shasta County Board of Supervisors meeting in November 2024 she briefly interrupted former supervisor Patrick Jones, who was criticizing the county elections office, then sat silently on the floor in front of the dais holding a political sign. She was charged with a misdemeanor under California Penal Code §403 (disrupting a public meeting).

After a weeklong jury trial in early 2026 she was convicted. Visiting Judge Thomas L. Bender (Madera County) offered her probation; the proposed conditions would have required her to follow Board-of-Supervisors meeting rules going forward. She refused, telling the court she could not in good conscience accept terms that conflicted with her First Amendment rights. On January 28, 2026 Judge Bender sentenced her to 90 days in the custody of the Shasta County Sheriff's Office, which she served as roughly 45 days of house arrest with an ankle monitor before being released in early March 2026. Her husband Benjamin lost his job over the family's protest activity. The case drew national attention as an early test of how aggressively local prosecutors can criminalize silent, sit-in–style protest at public meetings; Deputy DA Emily Mees prosecuted.

Sources: r/law (March 2026), The Guardian, Shasta Scout, KRCR, A News Cafe.

expected.name: Thomas Sims
expected.description: Thomas Sims was a Black man held in Boston federal custody under the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 after escaping enslavement in Georgia. The first major fugitive-slave rendition in Massachusetts under the 1850 Act; the courthouse was wrapped in chains by U.S. Marshals to prevent rescue by the Boston Vigilance Committee. Defended by Richard Henry Dana Jr. and Robert Rantoul Jr. Returned to Savannah on April 12, 1851, where his enslaver had him publicly whipped. On February 15, 1851 — while his lawyers awaited a court session — a Boston Vigilance Committee crowd of free Black Bostonians led by Lewis Hayden rushed the courthouse and freed him, hiding him in Beacon Hill before spiriting him to Montreal via the Underground Railroad. President Fillmore demanded prosecutions; juries acquitted all the rescuers. Minkins lived the rest of his life as a free man in Montreal, where he ran a restaurant and barber shop.

expected.name: Daniel Ellsberg

The leak revealed that successive administrations had systematically deceived Congress and the public about the war. Indicted on June 28, 1971 under the Espionage Act and related statutes; Ellsberg faced 115 years in prison. His May 1973 trial ended in a mistrial after the court learned of Nixon-administration misconduct (the "Plumbers" had burglarized his psychiatrist's office, illegally wiretapped him, and offered the trial judge the FBI directorship). Ellsberg spent the rest of his life as a leading anti-nuclear, antiwar, and whistleblower advocate, defending Chelsea Manning, Edward Snowden, and Julian Assange. Died June 16, 2023.

Charges as recorded: Conspiracy, espionage (Espionage Act of 1917), and theft of government property — for leaking the Pentagon Papers to the New York Times et al.

expected.name: Jogues Egan
expected.description: Sister Jogues Egan was a Roman Catholic nun and educator jailed for civil contempt in 1971 for refusing to testify before the federal grand jury in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania that investigated the Catholic antiwar left — the so-called East Coast Conspiracy to Save Lives, the alleged plot associated with Daniel and Philip Berrigan to raid draft boards and symbolically kidnap national security adviser Henry Kissinger. Egan refused to answer the grand jury questions on the ground that they were derived from illegal government wiretapping and electronic surveillance. Held in contempt by the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and ordered jailed until she testified or the grand jury expired, she carried her challenge to the Supreme Court, which in Gelbard v. United States (1972) upheld the right of grand jury witnesses to refuse to answer questions based on unlawful surveillance. Her resistance, alongside fellow Catholic activist Anne Walsh, made her a prominent figure of Catholic antiwar grand jury resistance.

expected.name: Nelson Johnson
expected.description: The Reverend Nelson Johnson was a veteran Black freedom organizer in Greensboro, North Carolina — a leader of the student movement at North Carolina A&T in the late 1960s and founder of the Greensboro Association of Poor People — who by 1979 was an organizer with the Communist Workers Party. On November 3, 1979 he helped lead the "Death to the Klan" march when Ku Klux Klansmen and American Nazis opened fire, killing five of his comrades in what became known as the Greensboro Massacre. Johnson was stabbed in the attack — and then arrested at the scene, held overnight, and charged with inciting to riot and resisting arrest; he ultimately faced seven charges arising from the day and was held under a bond twice that of any of the Klansmen, none of whom would be convicted. In November 1980 the rioting charges against Johnson and his fellow demonstrators were dropped. He went on to become a minister and, decades later, a driving force behind the Greensboro Truth and Reconciliation Commission, the first such body in the United States.

expected_cases.sentence:
Jailed at the scene and held under a bond twice that of any Klansman; the charges were dropped in 1980 (no conviction).

Verdict as recorded: No — the rioting charges against Johnson and his fellow demonstrators were dropped in November 1980 (while the Klan and Nazi shooters were acquitted by all-white juries).

expected.name: Allen Blitz
expected.description:
Allen Blitz — a marcher who returned fire as the Klansmen and Nazis opened fire — was one of the Communist Workers Party anti-Klan demonstrators charged with rioting after the November 3, 1979 Greensboro Massacre — the attack in which Ku Klux Klansmen and American Nazis shot and killed five CWP activists at a "Death to the Klan" march in Greensboro, North Carolina. In a striking inversion of justice, the gunmen were acquitted by all-white juries while the wounded and surviving demonstrators were the ones prosecuted. The rioting charges against the demonstrators were dropped in November 1980.

His jailing can be dated from a contemporary Workers Viewpoint report: he was arrested on May 2, 1980, after the felony-riot indictments came down — not at the massacre itself — and was still in jail on May 3 with his wife Dori and Lacie Russell after Nelson Johnson and Rand Manzella posted bond. On May 5 a judge reduced the remaining defendants' bail to $5,000 each, apparently permitting their release, making his time jailed approximately three days.

expected_cases.charges: Rioting — brought against an anti-Klan demonstrator after Klansmen and Nazis killed five Communist Workers Party activists at the November 3, 1979 Greensboro Massacre, while the gunmen themselves were acquitted.
expected_cases.sentence: Verdict as recorded: No — the rioting charges against the Greensboro demonstrators were dropped in November 1980.

She saw the jailings as part of an effort, as she put it, "to squeeze out a contract" from the union.

expected_cases.sentence: Twelve days in jail during the April 1978 Boston school-bus drivers strike. Contemporary May 19, 1978 reporting individually quotes Ewing and corrects the previously recorded 1977 year. Exact admission and release days remain unverified.

expected.name: Joe O'Sullivan
expected.description: Joe O'Sullivan was a business agent for the Carpenters union in San Francisco during the 1976 strike by city craft workers — the roughly five-week walkout of seventeen craft unions against the City and County of San Francisco in the spring of 1976. After the strike was defeated, the city's administration prosecuted the union officials who had led it, and several were convicted of violating antistrike injunctions. O'Sullivan, alone among them, did not appeal his sentence and served a four-day jail term. (In a parallel move, plumbers' union chief Joseph Mazzola was ousted from the San Francisco Airport Commission for his role in the strike.)

expected_cases.charges: Criminal contempt.
expected_cases.sentence:
Four days in jail (1976).

Verdict as recorded: Convicted of violating an antistrike injunction; served a four-day jail term (he did not appeal).

Charges as recorded: Criminal contempt for violating an antistrike injunction during the 1976 San Francisco city craft workers' strike, in which he was a Carpenters union business agent.

expected.name: Mary Beatrice Belfrage
expected.description: Mary Beatrice Belfrage was a British journalist and former wife of National Guardian editor Cedric Belfrage. Immigration authorities arrested her on a deportation warrant on August 17, 1953, took her to Ellis Island, fingerprinted her, and held her for several hours before releasing her on $2,000 bail. The charge alleged Communist activity in Los Angeles at least 15 years earlier.

expected_cases.charges: Civil deportation proceeding based on alleged Communist activity in Los Angeles
expected_cases.sentence: Held for several hours on Ellis Island on August 17, 1953 and released on $2,000 bail.

expected.name: Rosaura Revueltas
expected.description: Rosaura Revueltas was the Mexican actress who starred in the pro-union film Salt of the Earth. Immigration officers arrested her at the New Mexico filming location on February 25, 1953, questioned her about Communism, and confined her under armed guard in an El Paso hotel. She was released from custody on March 6 and returned to Mexico.

expected_cases.charges: Immigration proceeding alleging an improperly documented entry into the United States
expected_cases.convicted: No criminal conviction; returned to Mexico
expected_cases.sentence: Confined under armed guard from February 25 through March 6, 1953.

expected.name: Reuben Ship
expected.description:
Reuben Ship was a Canadian-born radio and television writer known for The Life of Riley. After he invoked the Fifth Amendment before the House Un-American Activities Committee, immigration officials ordered him deported for alleged Communist Party membership. Agents took him into custody in handcuffs on January 12, 1953 and deported him to Canada that day. He later answered McCarthyism with the CBC satire The Investigator.

expected_cases.convicted: No criminal conviction; deported to Canada
expected_cases.sentence: Taken into custody in handcuffs and deported to Canada on January 12, 1953.

expected.name: LaRue Spiker
expected.description: LaRue Spiker was a Louisville activist who, with Mary Louise Gilbert, urged white neighbors to accept the Wade family’s move into a segregated neighborhood. A grand jury indicted her for sedition on October 1, 1954 after segregationists bombed the Wades’ home. Spiker was jailed in lieu of $10,000 bond and released after nearly two weeks. The prosecution was later abandoned after the Supreme Court invalidated state sedition prosecutions preempted by federal law.

expected_cases.convicted: Not tried; prosecution abandoned after state sedition laws were held preempted
expected_cases.sentence: Jailed in lieu of $10,000 bond and released after nearly two weeks; exact release date unresolved.

expected.name: Elba Chase Nelson
expected.description: Elba Chase Nelson was a New Hampshire Communist organizer and the party’s 1938 candidate for governor. During the state attorney general’s anti-subversion investigation, a judge ordered her to answer questions and found her in contempt when she refused. She spent the nights of December 7 and 8, 1953 in the Valley Street Jail in Manchester before being released after purging the contempt.

expected_cases.charges: Contempt for refusing questions in the New Hampshire attorney general’s subversion investigation
expected_cases.sentence: Jailed for two nights, December 7–9, 1953, in the Valley Street Jail.

expected.name: Michael Quill
expected.description: Michael J. Quill was president of the Transport Workers Union. A Brooklyn grand jury indicted him on three criminal-libel counts on February 11, 1954 over union publications concerning a former organizer. Police booked him at the Butler Street station, and he pleaded not guilty before being paroled to his lawyer’s custody that day. The court dismissed the indictment in the interest of justice on January 14, 1958.

expected_cases.charges: Three counts of criminal libel arising from union publications
expected_cases.sentence: Booked and paroled to his lawyer’s custody on February 11, 1954.

expected.name: Anne Braden
expected.description: Anne Braden was a journalist and civil-rights organizer who helped Andrew and Charlotte Wade buy a home in a segregated white neighborhood near Louisville. Authorities arrested her on October 1, 1954 on Kentucky sedition charges and held her until her parents posted $10,000 bond on October 8. Her trial was repeatedly postponed, and the charge was dropped in November 1956 after the Supreme Court invalidated state sedition laws.

expected_cases.charges: Sedition under Kentucky law for civil-rights activity surrounding the Wade home purchase
expected_cases.convicted: Not tried; charge dismissed in November 1956
expected_cases.sentence: Held seven days before release on $10,000 bond.

expected.name: Louise Gilbert
expected.description: Louise Gilbert was a Church of the Brethren social worker active in interracial work in Louisville. She and LaRue Spiker urged white neighbors to accept the Wade family’s move into a segregated neighborhood. A grand jury indicted Gilbert for sedition on October 1, 1954 after segregationists bombed the Wades’ home. She was jailed in lieu of $10,000 bond and released after nearly two weeks. The prosecution was later abandoned.

expected_cases.sentence: Jailed in lieu of $10,000 bond and released after nearly two weeks; exact release date unresolved.

expected.name: Pete Seeger
expected.description: Pete Seeger, the folk singer, was cited for contempt of Congress in 1956 after refusing — on First Amendment grounds rather than the Fifth — to tell the House Un-American Activities Committee about his associations; he described himself to the committee as a 'banjo picker.' He was convicted in 1961 and the conviction was overturned in 1962.

expected_cases.charges: Contempt of Congress
expected_cases.convicted: Cited for contempt 1956; prosecution referred to the Justice Department
expected_cases.sentence: Sentenced April 4, 1961 to concurrent one-year terms for contempt of Congress. He was remanded when the trial judge refused continued bail, then freed on $2,000 appeal bail. Smithsonian Folkways documents that this detention lasted only a few hours; it contributes no complete day to the counter. The sentence must not be counted as a year actually served.

expected.name: John H. Calhoun
expected.description: John H. Calhoun was the head of Atlanta's NAACP, jailed for contempt in 1956 for refusing to hand over the organization's books to Georgia state revenue agents in the state's drive to tax the NAACP out of existence. He was released after four hours and given a one-year suspended contempt sentence by a judge who openly avowed segregationist views.

expected.name: Rosa Parks
expected.description: Rosa Parks was the Montgomery seamstress and NAACP secretary whose arrest on December 1, 1955 for refusing to surrender her bus seat helped launch the Montgomery bus boycott. Police booked her and released her on bail later that evening. She was convicted on December 5 and fined $10 plus $4 in court costs. On February 22, 1956, Parks voluntarily surrendered with other boycott leaders indicted under Alabama’s anti-boycott law and was released on bond the same day.

expected_cases.sentence: $10 fine and $4 in court costs; released on bail the evening of her arrest and did not serve a jail sentence.

expected.name: E. D. Nixon
expected.description: Edgar Daniel Nixon was a Pullman porter, union organizer, longtime NAACP leader, and a principal organizer of the Montgomery bus boycott. A grand jury indicted him and other boycott leaders on February 21, 1956 under Alabama’s anti-boycott law. Nixon reported for arrest on February 22, was booked and fingerprinted at the county jail, and was released on $300 bond the same day.

expected.name: Wilhelmina Jakes
expected.description: Wilhelmina Jakes was a Florida A&M College student whose May 26, 1956 arrest helped begin the Tallahassee bus boycott. Police accused Jakes and Carrie Patterson of placing themselves in a position to incite a riot after they sat beside a white passenger. They were booked and released on $25 bond pending a hearing that same day.

expected_cases.charges: Placing herself in a position to incite a riot for defying bus segregation
expected_cases.sentence: Booked and released on $25 bond on May 26, 1956.

expected.name: Hazel Wolf
expected.description: Hazel Wolf was an environmentalist, labor organizer, and Communist Party member in Seattle. Immigration authorities arrested her at her office on May 31, 1949 and held her for about four hours before releasing her on $500 bail. The government pursued deportation for years, but Wolf remained in the United States and later became a prominent conservation leader.

expected_cases.convicted: Ordered deported, but remained in the United States
expected_cases.sentence: Held for about four hours on May 31, 1949 and released on $500 bail.

expected.name: William Holmes Borders
expected.description: The Reverend William Holmes Borders was pastor of Atlanta’s Wheat Street Baptist Church and a leader of the Love, Law and Liberation Movement. Police arrested him on January 10, 1957 after he and five other Black ministers deliberately rode in seats reserved for white passengers to test Georgia’s bus-segregation law. He was fingerprinted and released on $1,000 bond that day.

expected_cases.sentence: Fingerprinting and same-day release on $1,000 bond.

expected.name: Judy Jenkins
expected.description: Judy Jenkins was a New Orleans civil-rights activist arrested with her husband Grady in 1957 under Louisiana's criminal-anarchy and anti-subversion laws for refusing to answer the Eastland subcommittee. The couple, parents of two small children, were prosecuted in what supporters called a Red-scare diversion tied to segregation politics.

expected.name: Daisy Bates
expected.description: Daisy Bates was the president of the Arkansas NAACP and a mentor to the Little Rock Nine. After city officials demanded the organization’s membership records, a warrant was issued on October 31, 1957. Bates surrendered on November 1, was booked, and posted $300 bond the same day. She was later convicted and fined, but the U.S. Supreme Court reversed the conviction on February 23, 1960.

expected.name: Robert Gillmore
expected.description: Robert Gillmore was the New York secretary of the American Friends Service Committee and chairman of the local Committee for Non-Violent Action. Police arrested him on May 6, 1958 with eight other demonstrators who refused to take shelter during a compulsory civil-defense drill to protest preparations for nuclear war. The court imposed a suspended thirty-day sentence, so he did not serve a jail term in this case.

expected_cases.charges: Refusing to take shelter
expected_cases.sentence: Thirty days, suspended; no jail term was served.

expected.name: Clennon Washington King Jr.
expected.description: Clennon Washington King Jr. was a Black college professor who in June 1958 tried to register for graduate study at the all-white University of Mississippi. State authorities seized him and committed him to the state mental hospital at Whitfield for a psychiatric examination — on the theory that any Negro who tried to integrate Ole Miss must be insane. No criminal charge was brought, because a charge would have required a court. A contemporary United Press International report says he was released on June 18, after twelve days, when hospital doctors pronounced him sane. Martin Luther King Jr. protested the confinement to Governor James P. Coleman. King later became the second African American man to run for President of the United States.

expected_cases.charges: No criminal charges — involuntary commitment to a state mental hospital (attempt to register at the University of Mississippi)
expected_cases.sentence: Held about 12 days in the state mental hospital at Whitfield

expected.name: Septima Clark
expected.description: Septima Poinsette Clark was Highlander Folk School’s education director and a leader of the citizenship-school movement. Tennessee officers arrested her during a raid on Highlander on the night of July 31, 1959 and jailed her in Grundy County on an accusation of possessing liquor. She was released early the next morning after a $500 cash bond was posted. The charge was never brought to trial and was later dropped.

Officers accused him of drunkenness, interfering with officers, and resisting arrest. expected.name: Wilmer Young
expected.description: Wilmer Young was a seventy-one-year-old Quaker from Wallingford, Pennsylvania, who joined the Omaha Action against construction of the Atlas missile base at Mead, Nebraska. A United States marshal arrested him after he climbed the base fence on July 6, 1959 and took him to the county jail. He pleaded guilty the next day and received a six-month sentence and $500 fine, both suspended on condition that he stay away from military installations.

expected.name: Mark Lane
expected.description:
Mark Lane was a New York State Assemblyman who joined the 1961 Freedom Rides and was arrested on an integrated bus ride and jailed in Jackson, Mississippi. He was sentenced to four months (two suspended) and a $200 fine for 'breach of the peace,' and appealed.

Lane went on to become one of the most prominent critics of the Warren Commission: his 1966 best-seller Rush to Judgment was the first major book challenging the official account of the Kennedy assassination. A lawyer to the end of his life, he later represented James Earl Ray before the House Select Committee on Assassinations, was in Jonestown as an attorney for the Peoples Temple when the 1978 massacre began and escaped into the jungle, and continued writing and litigating civil-rights cases until his death in Charlottesville, Virginia in 2016.

Four months (two suspended) and a $200 fine

expected.description: John Hardy was a twenty-one-year-old Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee field secretary working on voter registration in southwest Mississippi. On September 7, 1961, the Walthall County registrar struck Hardy over the head with a pistol after Hardy accompanied two Black residents to register. Officials then arrested Hardy for disturbing the peace and inciting a riot and confined him first in Tylertown and then in the jail at Magnolia. expected.description: William “Bill” Heikkila was a Finnish-born San Francisco draftsman brought to the United States as an infant. Agents seized him after work on April 18, 1958, took him through Canada, held him in the Vancouver city jail, and flew him to Finland while his court challenge remained pending. expected.name: Ida Rothstein
expected.description: Ida Rothstein was a Russian-born garment worker, union organizer, Communist Party activist, and secretary of the San Francisco Civil Rights Congress. Immigration authorities arrested her on January 9, 1951 in a deportation case and released her the same day on $5,000 bail. She claimed United States citizenship through her common-law marriage to an American citizen. Rothstein died on January 15, 1954 after being struck by a car.

expected_cases.charges: Civil deportation proceeding based on alleged Communist affiliation
expected_cases.sentence: Arrested and released on $5,000 bail on January 9, 1951.

expected.name: Debra White Plume
expected.description: Debra White Plume was an Oglala Lakota activist and water protector from the Pine Ridge Reservation. She joined the 1973 Wounded Knee occupation and later founded Owe Aku, an organization devoted to Lakota culture, treaty rights and environmental protection. On September 2, 2011, National Park Service officers arrested her outside the White House during an Indigenous-led protest against the Keystone XL pipeline. She was taken to the city jail, booked and released later that day.

expected_cases.charges: Failure to obey a lawful order during the Keystone XL protest outside the White House
expected_cases.sentence: Booked at the city jail and released later the same day.

expected.name: Winona LaDuke
expected.description: Winona LaDuke is an Ojibwe economist, environmentalist, and writer from the White Earth Nation, a co-founder of Honor the Earth, and twice the Green Party's U.S. vice-presidential nominee. She has led Indigenous land- and treaty-rights and anti-pipeline campaigns for decades, including the Standing Rock resistance to the Dakota Access Pipeline and opposition to Enbridge's Line 3. In July 2021 she was arrested and jailed for three days for civil disobedience at a Line 3 worksite in Minnesota; the charges were dismissed in 2023.

expected_cases.charges: Gross-misdemeanor trespass on a critical public-service facility and obstruction of legal process — Line 3 (Enbridge) pipeline protest, Wadena County, Minnesota
expected_cases.convicted: Jailed three days; charges dismissed in 2023 by a judge who cited the government's mistreatment of Indigenous people
expected_cases.sentence: Three days jailed (charges later dismissed)

expected.name: Grace Thorpe
expected.description: Grace Thorpe, also known as No Ten O Quah, was a Sac and Fox Nation activist, Women’s Army Corps veteran and daughter of athlete Jim Thorpe. She served as a publicist and negotiator during the occupation of Alcatraz and later worked against nuclear-waste storage on Native land. Shasta County officers arrested Thorpe with thirty-three other Native activists and supporters on June 6, 1970 during the Pit River Tribe’s occupation of land claimed by Pacific Gas & Electric at Big Bend, California. Officers carried Thorpe from the site and took the group to Redding for booking on trespass charges. The case was still pending in early 1971, but an exact release time and final disposition have not been located.

expected_cases.charges: Trespassing during the Pit River Tribe’s occupation of Pacific Gas & Electric land at Big Bend, California
expected_cases.convicted: Outcome not located; prosecution was pending in early 1971
expected_cases.sentence: Taken to Redding for booking on June 6, 1970; exact release time and final disposition have not been found.

expected.name: Bernie Whitebear
expected.description: Bernie Whitebear (born Bernard Reyes, 1937–2000), a Colville (Sinixt) activist, was a central leader of Seattle's Red Power movement. On March 8, 1970 he co-led the occupation of Fort Lawton to reclaim federal land for urban Native people; he was arrested in the military's forceful response and released the next day, then kept organizing. The campaign won a 99-year lease in Discovery Park, where he founded the United Indians of All Tribes Foundation and the Daybreak Star Cultural Center.

expected_cases.charges: Felonious riot (March 8, 1970 Fort Lawton occupation, Seattle)
expected_cases.convicted: Arrested and released the next day; no conviction documented. The occupation campaign succeeded politically with the Discovery Park land grant

expected.name: Greg Grey Cloud
expected.description: Greg Grey Cloud is a Crow Creek Sioux singer, educator, and activist from South Dakota, and co-founder of Wica Agli, a Native men's organization against domestic and sexual violence. On November 18, 2014, he was arrested by Capitol Police after singing a Lakota honor song from the U.S. Senate gallery as senators rejected the Keystone XL pipeline; all charges were later dismissed. In 2016 he led the horseback "Spirit Riders" during the Standing Rock / Dakota Access Pipeline resistance.

expected_cases.charges: Disrupting Senate proceedings (Lakota honor song from the Senate gallery
expected_cases.sentence: Detained for five hours after singing from the Senate gallery on November 18, 2014; released the same day. This is a brief detention, not a full-day prison sentence.

expected.name: Lyda Conley
expected.description:
Lyda Conley was a Wyandot lawyer — the first woman admitted to the Kansas bar — who fought for decades to stop the sale of the Huron Indian Cemetery in Kansas City, Kansas, where her parents were buried. With her sisters she built an armed shack, "Fort Conley," inside the cemetery and physically guarded the graves. She was arrested multiple times for interfering with city officials and in June 1937 served ten days in jail rather than pay a fine for defending the cemetery. In 1909 she became the first Native American woman to argue a case before the U.S. Supreme Court (Conley v. Ballinger). (Recorded as Eliza Burton "Lyda" Conley)

Note: Birth year approximate (circa 1869).

expected_cases.charges: Disturbance of the peace / interfering with city officials while physically guarding the Huron Indian Cemetery, Kansas City, Kansas (multiple arrests)
expected_cases.sentence:
Served ten days in jail (June 1937) rather than pay a fine; arrested several times over the cemetery

Verdict as recorded: Convicted of disturbing the peace (June 1937)

expected.name: Tillie Paul
expected.description:
Tillie Paul was a Tlingit missionary, educator, and Alaska Native-rights pioneer whose organizing helped seed the Alaska Native Brotherhood and Sisterhood. On November 7, 1922 she acted as interpreter to help Charlie Jones, a Tlingit man, cast a ballot at Wrangell, Alaska, and was criminally charged in 1923 with "inducing an Indian to vote." Her son, attorney William Paul, defended the case; after Jones was acquitted, her charges were dismissed — a foundational victory for Alaska Native voting rights. (Recorded as Matilda "Tillie" Paul Tamaree)

Note: Wrangell historical material notes her exact birth date is uncertain; commonly given as January 18, 1863.
expected.aka: Matilda Kinnon Paul Tamaree; Tillie Paul Tamaree
expected.body:
1920s remaining-entry review: The complete nine-page Alaska State Archives criminal case 794-KB was visually inspected. Page 7 is the executed warrant return: the deputy certifies arrest in Wrangell on March 24, 1923 and that he then held Tillie Paul Tamaree in custody. This is not the March 23 warrant-issuance date or the November 7, 1922 election date. Pages 2-3 contain the completed, sworn and approved $500 bail bond dated March 30, 1923, used here as the bail-release endpoint. A contradictory handwritten year on the reverse is resolved by the typed 1923 bond, indictment and filing stamps. Page 9 is the signed October 13, 1923 dismissal, correcting the inherited October 9 claim. Custody means marshal detention; no particular prison is asserted. The existing photograph is retained.

Source record

expected_cases.charges: Indicted/charged with "inducing an Indian to vote" (aiding and abetting illegal voting)
expected_cases.sentence: Arrested and held in marshal custody March 24, 1923; admitted to $500 bail on the completed bond dated March 30, 1923. Charges dismissed October 13, 1923.

expected.name: Grady Fuller
expected.description: Grady Fuller was a twenty-two-year-old member of the National Committee to Combat Fascism in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. Police arrested Fuller and fifteen-year-old Cary Coe on January 12, 1971 after accusing them of stealing meat from a delivery truck, an accusation the organization described as a pretext for raids on the Black community and its office. Fuller’s bail was set at $7,000. On March 19, 1973 he pleaded no contest to misdemeanor larceny and two misdemeanor assault charges. The court imposed ninety days and credited him with twelve days already served. The available record establishes those twelve days of confinement but does not identify their exact endpoints or show whether he served any balance of the sentence.

expected_cases.charges: Misdemeanor larceny and two misdemeanor assault charges arising from the January 1971 meat-truck case
expected_cases.convicted: Pleaded no contest to misdemeanor larceny and two misdemeanor assault charges
expected_cases.sentence: Ninety days, with credit for twelve days already served; the available record does not establish whether he served the remaining balance.

expected.name: Mark Edward Allen
expected.description: Mark Edward Allen was thirteen years old when Monrovia, California, police arrested him on suspicion of shoplifting a leather coat on November 16, 1971. Police booked Allen at 5:11 p.m. and confined him in cell M4 at the Monrovia Police Station. Officers reported finding him unresponsive at about 6:25 p.m. and said he had strangled himself with his pants. A Black police cadet said Allen had arrived shirtless, highly agitated and scratched across his body. Allen was pronounced dead at Arcadia Methodist Hospital. He spent a little more than one hour in the station before he was found unresponsive.

expected_cases.charges: Suspicion of shoplifting
expected_cases.convicted: No; died in police custody before prosecution
expected_cases.sentence: No sentence. Booked at 5:11 p.m. and found unresponsive at about 6:25 p.m. on November 16, 1971.

expected.name: LaSaunders Hudson
expected.description: LaSaunders Hudson was a Memphis dry-cleaning business owner who refused to pay state taxes as a protest against the uncompensated oppression of Black people. On June 15, 1972 he disarmed four revenue agents at his shop, made three leave without their clothes and held the fourth while demanding to meet Governor Winfield Dunn. After an eight-hour standoff Hudson met the governor and was taken into custody. He spent the night in the Memphis jail and was released on $2,000 bond on June 16. A kidnapping accusation was dropped, leaving a charge of assault with intent to murder; the final disposition has not been located.

expected_cases.charges: Assault with intent to murder arising from the June 15, 1972 tax protest; kidnapping accusation dropped
expected_cases.sentence: Held overnight in the Memphis jail and released on $2,000 bond on June 16, 1972.

expected.name: Kirk Taylor
expected.description: Kirk Taylor was a member of the San Francisco Black Caucus, arrested with co-chairman Larry Pinkney in 1972 when Berkeley police searched their car without a warrant. He was charged with carrying a concealed weapon and receiving stolen goods and held on $8,500 bond, jailed two days until the bond was reduced at his arraignment — at which, The Black Panther reported, it was made clear there was no case against him. Documented in The Black Panther (October 21, 1972).

expected_cases.charges: Carrying a concealed weapon and receiving stolen goods (San Francisco Black Caucus; held on $8,500 bond, then released for lack of a case)

expected.name: Aaron Dixon
expected.description: Aaron Dixon was a University of Washington Black Student Union leader who, after the March 1968 sit-in at Seattle's Franklin High School demanding Black teachers and curriculum, was arrested and convicted of unlawful assembly. He was sentenced to six months and briefly jailed in 1968, and shortly afterward became the founding captain of the Black Panther Party's Seattle chapter. The unlawful-assembly conviction was later challenged and prosecutors declined to retry it, so he never served the full term. He remains a living activist and author.

expected.name: Larry Gossett
expected.description: Larry Gossett was a Seattle Black Power and civil-rights activist who co-founded the University of Washington's Black Student Union after being radicalized as a VISTA volunteer in Harlem. On March 29, 1968 he co-led a sit-in at Seattle's Franklin High School (with Aaron Dixon and Carl Miller) protesting the treatment of Black students, and was arrested, convicted of unlawful assembly, and sentenced to six months in jail. The Washington Supreme Court later ordered a retrial and prosecutors declined to re-try the case, so the conviction was vacated. He went on to serve on the King County Council from 1994 to 2020.

expected.name: Kent Ford
expected.description: Kent Ford co-founded the Portland, Oregon chapter of the Black Panther Party in 1969. In June 1969 he intervened during a police arrest, was beaten, and was jailed for roughly two weeks at Rocky Butte Jail on a charge of inciting a riot, with bail set at $80,000 and paid by supporters. His rioting trial in early 1970 lasted nine days and ended in acquittal; he later won a settlement and successfully sued the Portland police in federal court over his treatment. He remains a living activist and Panther historian in Portland.

Authorities charged all three with misdemeanor stalking and felony intimidation of a state officer. Dupuis spent the first four nights in solitary confinement at Bartow County Jail and was released on bond in May. Georgia later included Dupuis in its 61-person Stop Cop City racketeering indictment; a Fulton County judge dismissed that RICO charge on December 30, 2025. The cited ruling did not dispose of the separately filed Bartow County flyer charges.

expected.name: Damean Martin
expected.description: Damean Martin was arrested in the early hours of July 4, 2022, in Akron, Ohio, during mass protests that erupted following the police killing of Jayland Walker, a 25-year-old Black man shot by Akron officers on June 27, 2022. Martin was among nearly 50 demonstrators swept up in what civil rights attorneys later characterized as baseless mass arrests, in which Akron police subjected peaceful protesters and bystanders to violence including beatings, tear gas, and pepper spray. He was charged with Riot (ORC 2917.03), Misconduct at an Emergency (ORC 2917.13), and Failure to Disperse (ORC 2917.04). Martin was transported to and detained at Summit County Jail, where protesters were held at least through the following day in overcrowded conditions — some chained together by wrists and ankles — and were denied medical care and access to phone calls. All charges against Martin were eventually dismissed after nearly a year of criminal litigation. In June 2023, Martin joined 23 other plaintiffs in a federal civil rights lawsuit filed in Ohio's Northern District court against the City of Akron and nearly 100 defendants, including Akron police officers, Summit County Sheriff deputies, and University of Akron officers, alleging unlawful arrest, excessive force, and malicious prosecution. The City of Akron settled the lawsuit for $747,000.

expected_cases.sentence: No sentence; released July 5, 2022. All charges dismissed by September 14, 2022.

expected.name: Pat McWhorter
expected.description: Pat McWhorter was one of the thirteen soldiers of the all-Black 24th Infantry Regiment hanged at Camp Travis, near San Antonio, at dawn on 11 December 1917, after the first Houston-riot court-martial (the "Nesbit case"). The executions were carried out in secret, within a day of sentencing and without the War Department review that would normally have allowed an appeal. The Houston riot of 1917 (the Camp Logan mutiny) erupted on 23 August 1917 after Houston police, enforcing Jim Crow, beat and arrested soldiers of the all-Black 24th Infantry Regiment. About 150 soldiers marched on the city; the night left some twenty people dead. In the largest court-martial in U.S. history, 118 men were tried, 19 executed, and 63 sentenced to life imprisonment. In 2023 the U.S. Army set aside all 110 convictions and honorably discharged the soldiers. (Recorded as Private Pat McWhorter)

expected_cases.charges: Mutiny; riot (August 23, 1917 Houston riot court-martial of the 24th Infantry Regiment)

Hanged at Camp Travis, near Fort Sam Houston, on 11 December 1917.

Verdict as recorded: Convicted by court-martial, 1917; conviction set aside by the U.S. Army in 2023

expected.name: Albert Weisbord
expected.description:
Albert Weisbord was arrested and jailed repeatedly through the strike year, held at one point under $30,000 bail and facing multiple indictments (including one for 'predicting the overthrow of the government' in a speech). The prosecutions were used as a club against the strike and were dropped as it wound down. He later founded the Communist League of Struggle.

Albert Weisbord was the young Harvard-trained organizer who led the great 1926 Passaic, New Jersey textile strike of 15,000 mill workers — the first mass strike led by American communists.
expected.body:
1920s custody review: Two April1926 detention episodes are distinguished. An April10 Associated Press dispatch reports the arrest and remand without bail. The April21 Daily Worker (April19 dispatch) and Textile Strike Bulletin describe a Saturday release and immediate rearrest, followed by Sunday release: April17 and18. The original year-only case now describes April10-17 detention; the April17-18 episode is separate. These were pretrial jailings, not a prison sentence.

Sources: Daily Iowan, April11,1926, page1; Daily Worker, April21,1926, page1; Textile Strike Bulletin, April21,1926.

Released on bail from the Paterson jail on Saturday April17, then rearrested that day in a separate Garfield proceeding. This is pretrial jail detention, not service of a prison sentence. Other strike-year jailings, if any, require individual dates.

expected_cases.charges: Garfield rearrest during the Passaic textile strike immediately following release on Paterson bail, April17,1926.
expected_cases.sentence: Rearrested and detained on Saturday April17,1926 after release in Paterson. Released again on $5,000 bail Sunday morning, April18. Contemporary sources agree on this sequence while differing on some other bail amounts. No continuous imprisonment beyond this bail release is inferred.

expected.description: Michael Palumbo was a New York anti-fascist who attended a Khaki Shirts rally in Astoria on July 14, 1933 with other opponents of the fascist organization. expected.name: Joseph Shoemaker
expected.description: Joseph Shoemaker was born in Philadelphia on February 24, 1888. He worked as an actor in Brooklyn and later lived in Bennington, Vermont, where he was active in the Socialist Party. He moved to Tampa in May 1935 and founded the Modern Democrats, campaigning for public ownership of utilities and jobs for the unemployed. Police arrested and briefly detained him during a political meeting on November 30, 1935. After his release, police and Ku Klux Klan members abducted him and two fellow organizers, beat them and applied hot tar to their bodies. Shoemaker was found injured the next morning and taken to Centro Español Hospital. He died there on December 9, 1935.

When they told him he was free, an officer forced him into a waiting car. Police and Ku Klux Klan members took him outside Tampa, flogged him, and tarred and feathered him. Poulnot survived and testified against his abductors.

expected.name: Whirlwind Larson
expected.description: Whirlwind Larson was a Chicago salesman for the Daily Worker and Sunday Worker who had immigrated to the United States in 1904. His attempts to obtain citizenship failed amid his labor activity and financial difficulties. After applying for permission to re-enter the country in 1934, he was summoned to a federal office, recognized as a labor-paper salesman, handcuffed and taken to the county jail for deportation proceedings. Larson was arrested at noon on a Thursday and freed at noon on Saturday after the International Labor Defense raised $1,000 cash bail. He then pledged to organize a neighborhood defense branch and raise money for other imprisoned workers.

Authorities released him on May 16 after requiring him to waive any false-arrest claim when no federal marshal appeared to take the case.

expected.name: Margaret McSurely
expected.description:
Civil-rights organizer arrested with her husband Al on sedition charges after organizing in eastern Kentucky; home raided, papers seized, and house bombed. The Black Panther Vol. 18 no.7 (1978); their case reached the U.S. Supreme Court. 

Margaret McSurely and her husband Al, field organizers for the Southern Conference Educational Fund, were arrested at their Pike County home on August 11, 1967 and charged under Kentucky’s sedition statute after a nighttime raid seized their books and papers. Within weeks a three-judge federal court in McSurely v. Ratliff held the statute unconstitutional and blocked the prosecution. Their seized papers were nonetheless passed to a U.S. Senate investigations subcommittee, launching the decade-long McSurely v. McClellan litigation over the raid and their subsequent contempt-of-Congress convictions (reversed on appeal); in December 1968 their home was dynamited. In 1983 a jury awarded the McSurelys $1.6 million in damages against the former Pike County prosecutor and federal officials.

expected_cases.sentence:
Verdict as recorded: No — statute held unconstitutional (McSurely v. Ratliff, 1967)

Charges as recorded: Sedition (Kentucky statute) — for books and papers seized in the August 1967 raid on their Pike County home

expected.name: Robert T. Begin
expected.description: Robert T. Begin was one of the D.C. Nine, who entered Dow Chemical’s Washington offices on March 22, 1969 and damaged files and equipment with blood to protest the company’s manufacture of napalm. Police arrested the group at the scene. They spent one week in the D.C. jail while fasting and posted bond on March 29. A jury convicted Robert T. Begin on February 11, 1970, and sentencing followed on May 6. The U.S. Court of Appeals reversed the convictions and ordered a new trial on June 30, 1972.

expected.description:

She became one of the world's leading agrostologists, and the Smithsonian holds her papers. (Recorded as Mary Agnes Chase; April 20, 1869 - September 24, 1963)

She served a ten-day sentence from August 15 to 20, 1918, released early with the rest of that group. A further five-day term followed in January 1919, but its exact dates remain unresolved.

Her birth date is April 20, 1869, per the Smithsonian record; April 29 appears in some accounts and is wrong.

expected.name: Elizabeth Green Kalb
expected.description:
Elizabeth Green Kalb was born in Columbus, Ohio, and was living in Houston, Texas at the time of her arrest. A graduate of Rice Institute in 1916 and a student at the University of Chicago, she was a member of the National Woman's Party and one of the "Silent Sentinels" imprisoned during the 1917-1919 campaign to picket the Wilson White House for woman suffrage. She died in Front Royal, Virginia. The exact days of her birth and death are unresolved. (1896-1973)

She was arrested on January 13, 1919 and released on bail that afternoon, then rearrested the same evening and held overnight in the House of Detention. On January 14 she was sentenced to five days and committed to the District of Columbia Jail. No discharge record has been found; the sentence would nominally have run to January 19, but that is a calculation rather than a record and is not entered as her release date.

expected.name: Annie J. Magee
expected.description:
Annie J. Magee was recorded among the members of the National Woman's Party jailed during the 1917-1919 campaign to picket the Wilson White House for woman suffrage. Doris Stevens's appendix gives her term as five days in January 1919.

Two identifications have been proposed and neither is established. Inez Haynes Irwin's history names a "Katherine Magee" arrested on January 27 and sentenced on January 28, 1919 to five days; whether that is the same woman as Annie J. Magee is not documented. Separately, Annie Josephine Stirlith McGee Jackson (May 4, 1873 - April 26, 1934) has been suggested as the person behind the name. Neither link can be made safely without a court or jail ledger, so no dates of birth, death or custody are recorded here and the two candidates are deliberately not merged into this record.

expected.description:
Gertrude Murphy was born about 1891 and was a member of the National Woman's Party jailed twice during the 1917-1919 campaign for woman suffrage. Her exact dates of birth and death are unresolved. (Recorded as Gertrude E. Murphy; later Gertrude Murphy Schneller and also spelled Sneller)

On January 16, 1919 she was sentenced to twenty-four hours for contempt after applauding suffrage prisoners in court, and served it in the District Jail. Arrested again on January 27 at a watchfire demonstration, she was sentenced on January 28 to five days in the District Jail and joined the hunger strike there.

No discharge record has been found for either term. The sentences would nominally have ended on January 17 and February 2, but those are calculations rather than records and are not entered as release dates.

expected.description:

expected.name: Ethel Byrne
expected.description: Ethel Byrne was a registered nurse and one of the three principal operators of the Brownsville birth-control clinic, the first in the United States, which opened at 46 Amboy Street in Brooklyn on October 16, 1916. Byrne, a trained nurse and the younger sister of Margaret Sanger, instructed women in contraceptive methods and supplied or demonstrated contraceptive articles. Police arrested her with Sanger and Fania Mindell on October 26, 1916 under New York Penal Law §1142, which forbade selling, giving away, possessing for distribution, or giving information about articles intended to prevent conception. Byrne spent the night at the Liberty Avenue police station in Brooklyn — Sanger and Mindell were held separately at Raymond Street Jail — and was released the next morning on $500 bail. Her trial opened in the Court of Special Sessions on January 4, 1917; the guilty verdict came on January 8 and was reported the following day, and on January 22 she was sentenced to thirty days in the Workhouse on Blackwell's Island. She entered custody the same day and announced that she would refuse both food and prison labour. A federal habeas corpus application brought her back from the island on January 23 before Judge Augustus N. Hand denied it, and she was placed in Cell 139, near the workhouse hospital, on January 24. Contemporary reporting says prison physicians began force-feeding her shortly before midnight on January 26, after roughly 106 hours without food, and that she had been fed by force about twelve times by February 1; the widely repeated figure of 185 unbroken hours without food or water is best understood as the length of her attempted fast overall, including the days she was being fed forcibly. Governor Charles S. Whitman pardoned her at about 7 p.m. on February 1, 1917, on the understanding that she would not break the law again — an assurance Margaret Sanger gave on her behalf, believing her sister close to death — and she was carried off Blackwell's Island at about 10:30 that night, having served about ten days of the thirty. Her documented custody in the case came to roughly eleven days, counting the night after her arrest. She was born in Corning, New York in 1883 and died in Massachusetts in 1955.

expected_cases.charges: Violation of New York Penal Code §1142 — as a registered nurse at the Brownsville clinic at 46 Amboy Street, instructing women in contraceptive methods and supplying or demonstrating contraceptive articles.
expected_cases.sentence:
Pretrial detention. Byrne was held overnight at the Liberty Avenue police station in Brooklyn — Sanger and Mindell were taken to Raymond Street Jail — and released the next morning on $500 bail. The clinic reopened on November 14, 1916 and Margaret Sanger was arrested again that day, but no surviving account places Byrne among those arrested, so this is her one documented clinic arrest.

Charges as recorded: Violation of New York Penal Code §1142 — as a registered nurse at the Brownsville clinic at 46 Amboy Street, instructing women in contraceptive methods and supplying or demonstrating contraceptive articles. Arrested with Margaret Sanger and Fania Mindell in the raid of October 26, 1916.

expected_cases.charges: Violation of New York Penal Code §1142 — distribution of a contraceptive article and related contraceptive instruction at the Brownsville clinic.
expected_cases.sentence:
Thirty days in the Workhouse on Blackwell's Island, imposed January 22, 1917, of which she served about ten. She entered custody the same day and refused food and prison labour. A federal habeas corpus application brought her back to court on January 23; Judge Augustus N. Hand denied it, and on January 24 she was placed in Cell 139 near the workhouse hospital. Forced feeding began shortly before midnight on January 26, after roughly 106 hours without food, and was repeated about twelve times by February 1. Governor Charles S. Whitman pardoned her at about 7 p.m. on February 1, 1917, conditional on her not repeating the offence, and she was removed from the island at about 10:30 that night. The sentence ended by pardon — not by completion and not by reversal of the conviction. Some sources date the release February 2 because the pardon was reported in that morning's papers and her care continued into the early hours; Dorothy Day's contemporaneous report in the New York Call puts the removal at 10:30 p.m. on February 1, which is the date used here.

Verdict as recorded: Yes — the guilty verdict came on January 8, 1917 (the day is reconstructed from the January 9 press report). The trial had opened on January 4 and sentencing was postponed to January 22.

expected.name: Ferruccio Coacci
expected.description: Ferruccio Coacci was an Italian anarchist born in Ancona in 1892. He immigrated to the United States in 1911, associated with Luigi Galleani and Cronaca Sovversiva, and lived in Bridgewater, Massachusetts, with his wife and two children. Federal authorities first arrested him in 1918 and later released him on bail. Police rearrested Coacci on April 16, 1920, and the federal government deported him to Italy on April 18. expected.name: Rose Fishstein
expected.description:
Rose Fishstein was a Philadelphia businesswoman and a member of the National Woman's Party, one of the "Silent Sentinels" imprisoned during the 1917-1919 campaign to picket the Wilson White House for woman suffrage. She was born in Russia, educated in New York and Philadelphia, and was a student at Temple University. She was arrested at a watchfire demonstration in February 1919 and sentenced to five days in the District Jail.

She was the sister-in-law of Rose Gratz Fishstein, who is also in this archive. Doris Stevens lists the two women as separate entries in Appendix 4 of Jailed for Freedom, one immediately after the other, and the shared forename and surname are why this record was missing: every automatic check for Rose Fishstein found Rose Gratz Fishstein and stopped.

expected_cases.charges: Arrested for picketing the Wilson White House for woman suffrage.
expected_cases.convicted: Imprisoned in the 1917-1919 National Woman's Party suffrage campaign
expected_cases.sentence:
Five days in the District Jail, which is the sentence Doris Stevens records.

NO DAY IS STORED, only the month. Stevens gives "Feb., 1919" for her where she gives February 9 for her sister-in-law, so neither the day she was taken in nor the day she came out is established. The women arrested at the February 9 watchfire demonstration were released together on February 13 after the hunger strike, which means the five days imposed may well not be the time actually served. The row carries a month-precision incarceration and no release date, and publishes no imprisonment figure.

expected.name: Henry Maki
expected.description:
Henry Maki was born Henrik "Heikki" Iivari Maentaka in Ähtäri, Finland. Henry Maki was a Finnish-American hard-rock miner and a member of the Western Federation of Miners in Telluride, Colorado. During the 1903-1904 Telluride strike, authorities arrested Maki and dozens of other unemployed strikers under a selectively enforced vagrancy law.

Thirty-four striking miners were taken in. Twenty-seven were convicted and ordered to pay $25 plus court costs, and given three choices: pay the fine, leave San Miguel County, or work under the sheriff's direction. The men produced $1,148.25 between them in open court and had their union behind them, which is the answer to the charge that they were destitute vagrants. The prosecutions were a mechanism for making strikers work, leave Telluride, or stay in jail.

Sixteen reported for the compulsory labour and were set to digging and repairing municipal sewers. Maki refused. Deputy sheriff Willard Runnels walked him to a telephone or telegraph pole, made him put his arms around it, and handcuffed his wrists together on the far side. Contemporary reports describe high wind, blowing snow and temperatures around zero. He was chained there for at least ninety minutes and possibly several hours before being returned to the cells, where a union history records that he was refused food for thirty-six hours. County Judge J. M. Wardlaw ordered the remaining vagrancy prisoners released on March 5, 1904.

A photograph of him chained to the pole became the central image of the Western Federation of Miners poster "Is Colorado in America?" The print on this record carries the line the union set beneath it: UNDER THE FOLDS OF THE AMERICAN FLAG IN COLORADO!

He went back to mining and was killed by falling rock at the Gold Pioneer Mine on August 17, 1910, aged 29.

THE ARREST DATE IS NOT SETTLED. One retrospective account puts the arrests on Monday, February 29, 1904, which is the date stored here. Emma Langdon's 1905 history of the strike places both the mass arrest and the justice-court proceedings on March 1. A wire report of March 2 says Maki and the others had been convicted "yesterday," which fixes the conviction on March 1 and is why that is recorded as the sentencing date. If Langdon is right about the arrest, the custody was four days rather than five.

expected_cases.charges: Vagrancy — selectively enforced against unemployed strikers during the 1903-1904 Telluride strike.
expected_cases.convicted: Yes — vagrancy, March 1, 1904; $25 and costs, or leave the county, or labour under the sheriff
expected_cases.judge: J. M. Wardlaw (county judge, ordered the release)
expected_cases.sentence: Arrested 1904-02-29 in the Telluride vagrancy sweep of thirty-four striking miners and convicted on March 1, 1904, one of twenty-seven; fined $25 plus costs with the alternatives of leaving San Miguel County or working under the sheriff. He refused the labour and on March 2 deputy sheriff Willard Runnels handcuffed him around a telephone or telegraph pole in high wind, blowing snow and temperatures near zero, where he was left at least ninety minutes. A union history records that he was then denied food for thirty-six hours. County Judge J. M. Wardlaw ordered the vagrancy prisoners released on March 5, 1904. Roughly five days in all. The custody was at Telluride city jail or the San Miguel County jail; the sources do not settle which, so no institution is recorded rather than the wrong one.

expected.name: Audrey Faye Hendricks
expected.description: Audrey Faye Hendricks was nine years old when she was arrested in Birmingham on May 2, 1963, the first day of the Children's Crusade, which makes her the youngest known person jailed in the American civil rights movement. She had walked out of Center Street Elementary alone — the only child from her school — and marched from the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church singing “Ain't Gonna Let Nobody Turn Me Round.” She was arrested for parading without a permit and held in the Juvenile Hall at the Birmingham city jail, sharing a bathroom with fifteen to twenty other girls. “I didn't have any fresh underwear or a change of clothes or a toothbrush,” she said later. She and some five hundred other children were released on Wednesday, May 8. She went back to school the next day and nobody asked her about it: “I was just one of the kids, as everybody else was. It didn't dawn on me that it was a big deal.” Both her parents were in the movement — her mother, Lola Mae Hendricks, worked out of Fred Shuttlesworth's office and with the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. She became a teacher, and died in Birmingham in 2009.

expected.name: John J. Warner
expected.description: John J. Warner was a tenant farmer in the anti-rent community on Blenheim Hill, New York. His daughter later described his imprisonment and the family's opposition to the rents demanded by the landlords.

expected_cases.charges: Detention during the 1845 Anti-Rent War crackdown; formal charge not established

The week refers to the Schoharie confinement, not the total including the church. Exact arrest and release days, the formal charge and any imposed sentence remain unverified. Source: Albert C. Mayham, The Anti-Rent War on Blenheim Hill (1906), pp. 83–84, recollection of Mrs. N. K. Hoagland, his daughter. https://archive.org/download/cu31924030043131/cu31924030043131_djvu.txt The incarceration year is recorded with year precision; January 1 is a storage placeholder, not an established admission day.

expected.name: Taylor Breann Enterline
expected.description: Taylor Breann Enterline is a racial-justice protester arrested in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, in September 2020 after the police killing of Ricardo Muñoz. She spent three days in pretrial custody. A jury later convicted her of riot and four related offenses but acquitted her of conspiracy. She received probation in 2023, and the judgment was affirmed in 2024. She maintained that her protest was peaceful.

expected_cases.charges: Riot; failure to disperse; obstruction of highways; disorderly conduct; defiant trespass
expected_cases.convicted: Jury conviction January 19, 2023; acquitted of conspiracy to commit riot
expected_cases.sentence: Three years of probation imposed April 4, 2023, with restitution and community service; affirmed May 31, 2024. The qualifying imprisonment was September 2020 pretrial detention, not the probation term. The appellate court rejected her sufficiency and weight challenges; it did not require proof that she personally threw or broke objects.

Prosecutors withdrew the felony charges and acknowledged that she had not thrown objects at officers.

expected_cases.charges: Failure to disperse; obstructing highways; disorderly conduct; trespassing

expected_cases.sentence: Eighteen months of probation, a fine and 100 hours of community service. The prison database records her September 2020 pretrial detention, not probation as jail time. The exact sentencing day is not entered.

She served six days in the Camden County Jail after a January 1989 protest at the Kings Bay Trident base in Georgia and continued organizing against nuclear weapons for decades afterward.

expected.body:
1920s remaining-entry review: The Daily Worker of March 14, 1924, pages 1 and 3, names Minnie Seidel with Morris Kravis and Eugenia Schlacter as the three garment strikers arrested the previous day by deputy sheriffs and brought before Judge Denis Sullivan for alleged violation of the Graceline Dress Company injunction. This supplies March 13, 1924 as the reported arrest date. The continuation describes bail of $500 each; the arrest must not be treated as the beginning of continuous imprisonment through her later five-day jail term. The June 22, 1926 report and named photograph caption support the existing release and photograph. The exact admission day for the 1926 term remains unverified; June is retained at month precision rather than calculated backward from five days.

expected.description: John Frank Cardiello, known as Frank, was a Catholic Worker organizer, psychiatric nurse practitioner, and peace activist. Issue 13 acknowledges conflicting reports, so its forward sentencing forecast is not treated as an actual prison admission. expected.name: Lorena Barnum Sabbs
expected.description:
Lorena Barnum Sabbs was one of the Black school-aged girls imprisoned in southwest Georgia in 1963 after participating in demonstrations against racial segregation in Americus. Authorities moved girls arrested during the campaign to the Lee County Stockade in neighboring Leesburg, concealed their location from their families, and held them without formal criminal charges. Her individual custody duration is documented in a contemporary sworn statement or closely contemporaneous record. The children endured overcrowding, inadequate food and water, broken sanitation, little or no bedding, and delayed medical attention. SNCC photographer Danny Lyon documented the confinement through the bars; publication of his photographs helped force public attention and the girls’ release.

Her September 13, 1963 sworn statement says she was 11 and confined in the stockade from August 31 to September 1. She described 32 children sharing two drinking cups, unusable toilets, and rusty-tasting water.

Photo: Servant Emannu'el Branch / BHBP News, September 27, 2019. Original-image crop; identified by the source (first of five survivors in foreground, from left). Source: https://bhbpnews.com/historical-marker-for-stolen-girls-held-at-leesburg-ga-stockade-p518-203.htm . Copyright status unconfirmed; used for educational biographical identification at the site owner's direction. No permission or open license claimed.
expected.body:
## The Leesburg Stockade

In the summer of 1963, young people in Americus, Georgia demonstrated against segregation, including the Martin Theater’s separate entrances and ticket windows. Local authorities arrested hundreds of participants. More than 30 Black girls were held at different times in the Lee County Stockade in nearby Leesburg without formal charges or a court hearing.

Contemporary sworn statements show that the girls did not all enter or leave together. They describe changing populations of roughly 32 to 35 children, overflowing or unusable toilets, contaminated bedding, undercooked food, rusty water, and periods when the children slept directly on concrete. The profile’s custody dates and duration are therefore individual where evidence permits; no universal 45-day range has been imposed.

SNCC photographer Danny Lyon photographed the girls and the stockade conditions. The resulting photographs circulated through movement publications and the Black press and helped expose where the children were being held.

expected_cases.charges: No formal criminal charges; detained after participating in civil-rights demonstrations against racial segregation in Americus, Georgia
expected_cases.convicted: No — never formally charged or brought before a judge
expected_cases.sentence: Held without formal charges for at least 24 hours.
