expected.name: Christopher Ruff
expected.description: Christopher Ruff is an Arizona First Amendment auditor who publishes police encounters under the name Direct D. Beginning in 2021, he recorded and livestreamed officers conducting investigations in Mesa and other Phoenix-area cities. In October 2022, a Mesa municipal judge sentenced him to at least five days in jail in four cases arising from police-scene filming and entry into a restricted part of Mesa City Plaza. The sentence included 180 suspended days and three years of probation, with a condition barring him from approaching or recording Mesa police investigations. Ruff said he was being punished for protected speech and planned to appeal; the judge said the punishment addressed interference, escalation, and repeated violations rather than recording alone.
expected.body:
## Mesa filming cases

Ruff began regularly recording police activity in 2021 and described the work as an effort to test First Amendment protections and hold officers accountable. Four Mesa cases reached sentencing together in October 2022. They involved encounters in which officers said he remained too close to active investigations or refused directions to move, and an incident in which he entered a restricted stairway inside Mesa City Plaza after being told not to.

Municipal Judge Raymond Schumacher ordered at least five days in jail, imposed 180 suspended days, and placed Ruff on probation for three years. One probation condition prohibited him from going to areas where Mesa police were investigating or recording Mesa officers during the probation period. Ruff argued in court that filming and verbally challenging police were protected speech and said he intended to appeal. Schumacher said Ruff’s recording by itself was not the basis for punishment, but found that his conduct deliberately escalated the encounters and interfered with officer safety and investigations.

## Source

- [East Valley Tribune via Police1: “Ariz. ‘guerilla journalist’ jailed for police filming, accessing restricted areas”](https://www.police1.com/legal/articles/ariz-guerilla-journalist-jailed-for-police-filming-accessing-restricted-areas-KaHT2GUQGxWWT66X/)

*Profile image: video still published with the East Valley Tribune report; Facebook via Gilbert Sun News.*

expected_cases.sentence: At least five days in jail, 180 suspended days, and three years of probation with restrictions on approaching and recording Mesa police investigations

expected.name: Paul Ervin Johnson
expected.description: Paul Ervin Johnson was a Minneapolis contractor who documented and protested federal immigration operations during Operation Metro Surge. On January 22, 2026 he followed federal agents in his van and stopped to observe them in a north Minneapolis parking lot. The government alleged that he approached their vehicle with a baseball bat and later sprayed pepper spray; Johnson said masked agents pulled him from the van and beat him unconscious, causing a traumatic brain injury and torn rotator cuff. Agents kept him shackled to a hospital bed for five days without access to his phone. Prosecutors first filed a felony assault complaint and later reduced the case to a misdemeanor. After defense filings challenged the agents’ account and affidavits, the government moved to dismiss. The court dismissed the case with prejudice in July 2026.

expected.name: Napoleon Jones
expected.description: Napoleon Jones is a US Navy veteran who recorded a police traffic stop in Sussex, Wisconsin, on May 4, 2025. Deputies subsequently stopped his vehicle, handcuffed him and took him to Waukesha County Jail. Reporting describes five hours in custody before release without citations or criminal charges. His federal civil-rights complaint alleges that the stop and arrest were retaliation for recording police. The complaint reproduces a sheriff's supervisor memorandum acknowledging that the traffic stop was unlawful and Jones could not be compelled to identify himself. Jones also alleges that deputies later used Flock license-plate searches to track his vehicle in retaliation for his complaint. Those retaliation claims are allegations in his civil lawsuit, not findings of a final judgment.

Reason, September 2, 2026, independently reports the five-hour custody period. No prison sentence imposed. The detention is not rounded to a full day in the imprisonment counter; the civil lawsuit is separate from this arrest case.

She told the Chicago Tribune that federal agents held her for approximately eight hours and released her without charges. A court-filed CBP arrest chart independently records her arrest and lists prosecution as declined.

expected_cases.charges: Federal officers recorded an allegation under 18 U.S.C. 111; prosecution declined
expected_cases.sentence: Approximately eight hours detained, according to her interview with the Chicago Tribune; released without charges. No conviction or sentence. Exact release time and calendar date are not specified and remain unset. Sources: https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/staff-chicago-tribune (reproduced Tribune reporting, Staged photo shoot section); https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.ilnd.487571/gov.uscourts.ilnd.487571.284.40.pdf (page 1, October 3 arrest and Declined disposition). The chart historical custody flag is not used to infer current status; actual release is documented by the interview. Her husband Michael Boyte reported being tackled but not detained or charged and is not added as a prisoner from this event.

expected.name: Scott Sakiyama
expected.description: Scott Sakiyama is an Oak Park attorney detained by federal immigration agents on October 20, 2025 while following their vehicles and warning neighbors with his horn and a whistle. He told the Chicago Tribune that agents held him for about an hour, largely in a parked van outside the Broadview facility, then returned him to his car with a citation. He disputed their allegation that he cut off their vehicle.

expected_cases.charges: Violation notice alleging interference with federal officers under 18 U.S.C. 111(a)
expected_cases.sentence: Approximately one hour in federal custody; released with a citation. No sentence or conviction established by the reviewed sources. Subsequent citation outcome and exact release calendar date remain unset. Sources: https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/staff-chicago-tribune (Tribune interview, Bizarre behavior section); https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.ilnd.487571/gov.uscourts.ilnd.487571.284.40.pdf (page 2, Scott Tadashi Sakiyama, October 20). The historical chart custody flag is not used to establish present custody; actual release is supported by his interview.

expected.name: Jennifer Moriarty
expected.description: Jennifer Moriarty is an Evanston attorney detained by federal immigration agents on October 31, 2025 after approaching with her phone to record their treatment of a motorist following a collision. She described being tackled, handcuffed and driven around in an SUV. She told the Chicago Tribune that she was allowed to leave more than five hours later at an FBI field office. A federal court opinion independently records her detention and release without charges.

expected_cases.charges: Released without charges
expected_cases.sentence: More than five hours detained, according to her Chicago Tribune interview; released without charges. No conviction or sentence. Exact release calendar date remains unset. Sources: https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/staff-chicago-tribune (Bizarre behavior section); https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/illinois/ilndce/1:2025cv12173/487571/281/ (November 20, 2025 opinion, pages 154-157). The opinion discusses the three Evanston detainees collectively and identifies Moriarty individually. Its injunction was subsequently stayed and the underlying suit voluntarily dismissed; the profile does not present that injunction as currently operative.

expected.name: Rosemarie Dominguez
expected.description: Rosemarie Dominguez is a Little Village community activist and Chicago 10th District police council member. She told the Chicago Tribune that federal agents detained her on November 6, 2025 while she followed their vehicles and alerted community members to their presence. She reported approximately four hours in custody before release with a violation notice at the Broadview facility. She appeared in federal court on December 8 to contest the allegations.

expected_cases.charges: Federal violation notice; specific statutory charge not established in reviewed sources
expected_cases.sentence: Approximately four hours in custody, followed by release with a violation notice, according to her Tribune interview. No conviction or sentence established. The later citation outcome and exact release calendar date remain unset. Sources: https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/staff-chicago-tribune (December 30, 2025 Tribune reporting, Ticketed section); https://ccpsa.chicago.gov/district-council/10th-district-council/ (official council identity). Her account of agents firing pepper-spray projectiles at her vehicle and pushing her toward traffic is attributed testimony, not a separately adjudicated finding.

expected.name: Marcello Africano
expected.description: Marcello Africano is a U.S. citizen detained by federal immigration agents in Evanston on October 31, 2025 after approaching a collision scene while helping his brother move nearby. The Illinois Accountability Commission identified his detention as an example of force against observers and found reasonable cause to believe agents used unjustified force against him. Its April 2026 report records release after approximately five and a half hours and states that a charge of assaulting a federal officer was later dismissed.

expected_cases.charges: Assaulting a federal officer; later dismissed according to the Illinois Accountability Commission
expected_cases.sentence: Approximately five and a half hours detained; released at FBI headquarters. The commission reports a later dismissal, without specifying its date or procedural basis. No sentence. Exact release and dismissal dates remain unset. Source: https://ilac.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/ilac/documents/final-report/IAC-Final-Report-April-2026.pdf (pages 86-89 and 96). The commission finding is reasonable cause, not a criminal conviction of the officers.

expected.name: Armando Garnica
expected.description: Armando Garnica is a U.S. citizen arrested by federal agents during the October 14, 2025 protest in Chicago’s East Side neighborhood following an immigration-enforcement vehicle pursuit and collision. Agents alleged that he pushed through their perimeter while another person was being arrested. Their incident report records his transport to the FBI building and subsequent release without an assault charge at that time. The Illinois Accountability Commission separately documented same-day release of the three U.S. citizens arrested during the protest.

expected_cases.charges: Agents alleged assault or interference with a federal operation; released without an assault charge in the contemporaneous report
expected_cases.sentence: Detained and transported to the FBI, then released the same day. No conviction or sentence established; exact duration and any subsequent prosecution remain unverified. Sources: https://www.loevy.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/284-25-ESTAR-Incident-Report-10.14.2025.pdf (pages 28, 55-56 and 58); https://ilac.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/ilac/documents/final-report/inv-briefs/IAC-East-Side-Investigation-Brief-r.pdf (page 5). Agent allegations are not recorded as proven facts. Birth year 2006 is visible in the original report; month and day are redacted. He is not identified as the separate unnamed Walgreens detainee solely because their ages overlap.

expected.name: Stephen Donaldson
expected.description: Stephen Donaldson, born Robert A. Martin Jr., was a writer, bisexual-rights activist and advocate against sexual assault in prisons. NYPL’s archive biography records his arrest at a Quaker peace protest at the White House in 1973 and subsequent confinement in the Washington, D.C. jail, where he was sexually assaulted. In a recollection published by Brown University, Beth Taylor links Robert Martin to Donaldson and describes the protest against the bombing of Cambodia, his decision not to pay $10, and the Quaker community’s help in securing his release. Just Detention International independently identifies the peace-protest arrest and jail experience as central to his later advocacy. This case concerns that antiwar protest detention. His later felony imprisonment and parole violation are separate episodes and are not represented as imprisonment for the 1973 protest. NYPL records his birth on July 27, 1946, and death in New York City on July 18, 1996.
expected.aka: Robert A. Martin Jr.; Robert Martin; Don Tucker; Donny the Punk
expected.body: Verified detail sources (October 9, 2026): NYPL’s archival biography identifies Stephen Donaldson as Robert A. Martin Jr., uses he/him, and records arrest at a Quaker White House peace protest and subsequent Washington, D.C. confinement in 1973. Both case dates are recorded with year precision. His later criminal imprisonment is a separate episode. Source 1.

expected_cases.charges: Arrest at 1973 Quaker peace protest at the White House; exact statutory charge unverified
expected_cases.sentence: Pretrial custody in District of Columbia Jail from August 14 through August 23, 1973 after the White House pray-in and refusal to post $10 bail. Released eight hours after Lucy Witt paid bail on August 23. Tried September 28 and acquitted October 1, 1973. This case excludes his separate overnight detention following the August 9 White House protest. No prison sentence imposed in this proceeding.

expected.name: Daniela Vargas
expected.description: Daniela Vargas is a Mississippi immigrant-rights advocate who previously received DACA protection. ICE detained her on March 1, 2017, shortly after she spoke at a Jackson news conference about immigration enforcement and her family's arrests. Her legal team alleged retaliation for protected speech. She was released under an order of supervision on March 10, 2017; release did not itself resolve the removal order. This is a historical detention record.
expected.body:
Case history and verification

Daniela Vargas is a Mississippi immigrant-rights advocate who previously received DACA protection. ICE detained her on March 1, 2017, shortly after she spoke at a Jackson news conference about immigration enforcement and her family's arrests. Her legal team alleged retaliation for protected speech. She was released under an order of supervision on March 10, 2017; release did not itself resolve the removal order. This is a historical detention record.

Status reviewed October 8, 2026: Historical case. The profile records the last documented outcome; no current ICE custody is asserted.

Sources

  • ABC News: March 10 release under supervision

Verified detail sources (October 8, 2026): ABC News’s March 10, 2017 account uses she/her for Daniela Vargas and identifies the March 1 Jackson press-conference arrest. The reported age of 22 is historical and is not converted to a birthdate. Source 1.

Photo source: Autostraddle, via Jackson Free Press. Photo by Imani Khayyam / Jackson Free Press. Source image reproduced without further alteration.

expected_cases.charges: Civil immigration detention and threatened removal; speech retaliation alleged by her lawyers.

expected.name: Jean Montrevil
expected.description: Jean Montrevil is a Haitian immigrant-rights organizer and co-founder of New Sanctuary Coalition. ICE detained him in January 2018 and deported him to Haiti. He sued federal officials, alleging that they targeted his constitutionally protected advocacy. Montrevil returned to the United States on special-interest parole in October 2021. In January 2022 his representatives announced that his immigration case would be reopened. Historical deportation is not represented here as ongoing ICE detention or confirmed present exile.
expected.body:
Case history and verification

Jean Montrevil is a Haitian immigrant-rights organizer and co-founder of New Sanctuary Coalition. ICE detained him in January 2018 and deported him to Haiti. He sued federal officials, alleging that they targeted his constitutionally protected advocacy. Montrevil returned to the United States on special-interest parole in October 2021. In January 2022 his representatives announced that his immigration case would be reopened. Historical deportation is not represented here as ongoing ICE detention or confirmed present exile.

Status reviewed October 8, 2026: Historical case. The profile records the last documented outcome; no current ICE custody is asserted.

Sources

  • NYU Immigrant Rights Clinic: return to the United States, October 18, 2021
  • Families for Freedom: immigration case reopening, January 2022

Verified detail sources (October 8, 2026): The July 19, 2021 NYU/Cornell civil-rights complaint, page 20, dates the arrest and immediate detention to January 3, 2018. NYU’s October 18, 2021 release identifies Montrevil as a father. No deportation day is added in this pass. Source 1. Source 2.

Verified detail sources (October 9, 2026): The January 31, 2019 amended Migrant Justice complaint, paragraph 139, explicitly dates Jean Montrevil’s deportation to January 16, 2018. The 2021 NYU/Cornell complaint independently describes removal on the next business day after the January 12 BIA decision. This date ends the U.S. detention episode through deportation; it is not ordinary release into the United States. Source 1. Source 2.

Photo source: Center for Constitutional Rights, 2010 Annual Report, printed page 22. Photo © New Sanctuary Movement. Original image reproduced without alteration.

expected_cases.charges: Civil immigration detention and deportation based on a prior conviction; First and Fifth Amendment violations alleged in a civil lawsuit.

expected.name: José Enrique Balcázar Sánchez
expected.description: José Enrique Balcázar Sánchez is a Vermont farmworker organizer with Migrant Justice. ICE detained him on March 17, 2017, after a group meeting. His lawsuit alleged surveillance and retaliation for organizing. He was subsequently released. A 2020 settlement protected three organizers from deportation for five years and included compensation, without a government admission of wrongdoing.
